239.title: A teacher and a friend (Avot 1:6)
239.hook: get yourself a teacher, gain a companion, and judge everyone favorably
239.carry: judge on the side of merit
239.howItsDone: Traditional Jewish study is often done in a chavruta, a pair of study partners who read and argue together, and dan lechaf zechut, judging others favorably, is counted among the everyday duties between people.

segments.voice: Yesterday, patuach lirvacha: a house open wide, where the poor are members of the household. Your line was open the door wide. Today, the next pair of teachers, and three things everyone needs. Day two hundred thirty-nine.

A friend texts, I need to talk, and then goes silent for six hours. A coworker walks past without saying hi. Your brother forgets your birthday. Each time, your brain writes a story in about half a second. They're angry at me. They're rude. He doesn't care. Sometimes the story is right. Often, it isn't. The phone died. She was crying in the stairwell. He's drowning at work. The next teacher in Avot's chain, Joshua ben Perachyah, gives three pieces of advice, and the last one is about that story in your head.
screen: `I NEED TO TALK. THEN SILENCE.` → `THE STORY IN HALF A SECOND.` → `JOSHUA BEN PERACHYAH.`

segments.voice: Joshua ben Perachyah says, in paraphrase: make for yourself a teacher, acquire for yourself a friend, and judge every person favorably. Look at the verbs. Make a teacher, not find one: even if no perfect teacher appears, choose someone and make them your teacher. Acquire a friend: the Hebrew kneh means buy. A real friend costs you something: time, patience, the humility to be corrected. An early companion to Avot says a true friend is someone you eat with, study with, and trust with your secrets. Jewish learning built this into its method. Students study in pairs, a chavruta, arguing over every line. Now the third: judge every person favorably. In Hebrew, lechaf zechut, on the side of merit. Picture a scale. When you don't know why someone did something, tip it toward the good reading. The Talmud tells a story about it. A man works three years for a farmer. On the eve of the holiday he asks for his wages. No money, the farmer says. Then give me produce. I don't have any. Land? Cattle? Blankets? None. The worker goes home empty-handed. After the holiday the farmer arrives with his wages and gifts, and asks: what did you think when I said I had nothing? Each time, the worker had imagined an innocent reason. And he was right: the farmer had pledged all his property to the Temple, and had it undone. The farmer says: as you judged me favorably, may God judge you favorably.

Lechaf zechut. On the side of merit: Joshua ben Perachyah's call to judge every person favorably, tipping the scale toward the good reading.
Your line: judge on the side of merit. A teacher, a friend, and a generous scale. That's day two hundred thirty-nine.

240.title: Choose your neighbors (Avot 1:7)
240.hook: Nittai: keep far from a bad neighbor, and don't give up on justice
240.carry: kindness isn't the same as closeness
240.howItsDone: Jewish teaching gives weight to choosing one's community and surroundings, and Nittai's advice is cited when people choose a neighborhood, a school or friends.

segments.voice: Yesterday, lechaf zechut: Joshua ben Perachyah said make a teacher, acquire a friend, and judge on the side of merit. Today, his partner, Nittai, adds the other side. Day two hundred forty.

Spend a week with a friend who complains about everything, and the complaining can rub off. Sit near the coworker who cuts corners, and your corners start getting shorter. Scroll a certain feed for an hour, and you come away a little meaner than you went in. People catch moods and habits from those around them, the way they catch colds. Joshua ben Perachyah said judge everyone favorably. His teaching partner, Nittai of Arbel, answers with a warning: being generous about people doesn't mean living next door to everything.
screen: `WE CATCH HABITS LIKE COLDS.` → `A LITTLE MEANER THAN BEFORE.` → `NITTAI OF ARBEL.`

segments.voice: Nittai of Arbel says three things, in paraphrase. Keep far from a bad neighbor. Don't attach yourself to a wicked person. And don't give up on justice; or, more literally, don't despair of retribution. Start with the neighbor. The advice is practical: when you choose where to live, who to work beside, who to be close to, choose with care. Rashi, reading a detail in the book of Numbers, notices who camped next to whom in the desert. The tribe camped beside a famous rebel was drawn into his rebellion. The tribes camped beside Moses grew great in learning. And Rashi passes on a saying: woe to the wicked, and woe to his neighbor; good for the righteous, and good for his neighbor. These two sayings sit side by side in Avot, from a pair of teachers. Judge everyone favorably. Keep far from a bad neighbor. Avot keeps both. You can give someone the benefit of the doubt and still choose not to sit next to them every day. Kindness isn't the same as closeness. Then the third line: don't despair of retribution. Commentators hear it two ways. Don't envy people who seem to get away with harm; justice isn't finished yet. And don't get complacent yourself when things go well; nobody's beyond consequences. Either way, Nittai is saying the world has a moral shape, even when it's hard to see.

segments.voice: Think about what you're close to every day, people, places, feeds, habits, group chats, and whether one reliably leaves you worse: not a person to condemn, just a neighbor to move away from. Picture putting a little distance there, muting it, sitting elsewhere, spending the time somewhere better. Then think of one good neighbor to move toward.
Nittai, the sage who taught keep far from a bad neighbor, and don't give up on justice, paired beside his partner's call to judge everyone favorably.

241.title: Careful words (Avot 1:9)
241.hook: Simeon ben Shetach: question witnesses well, and guard your words so no one learns to lie
241.carry: a question can teach a lie
241.howItsDone: Jewish law built strict rules for testimony on this teaching: witnesses are questioned separately and closely, and Avot 1:9 is also read as a guide to honest speech well beyond the courtroom.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nittai of Arbel: keep far from a bad neighbor, and don't give up on justice. Your line was kindness isn't the same as closeness. Day two hundred forty-one.

A kid is standing in the kitchen with crumbs on his shirt, and a parent asks, you didn't take the last cookie, did you? And the kid, who is not a fool, says no. The question handed him the answer. It told him which story would get him out of trouble. Questions like that get asked at home, at work, in a group chat. Long ago, a judge in Jerusalem noticed the same thing in a courtroom, where the stakes were a lot higher than a cookie.
screen: `CRUMBS ON HIS SHIRT.` → `THE QUESTION HANDED HIM THE ANSWER.` → `A JUDGE IN JERUSALEM.`

segments.voice: The judge is Simeon ben Shetach, who with his partner Judah ben Tabbai makes up one of the pairs of teachers in the chain of Pirkei Avot. He led the court in a stormy time, and later tradition remembers him as fearless in front of kings. His saying, in chapter one, comes in two halves. First: examine the witnesses thoroughly. The Torah says a matter is established by two or three witnesses, and Simeon wants them questioned hard, because a careless court convicts the innocent. Then the surprising half: and be careful with your words, so that they don't learn from them to lie. That half isn't aimed at the witnesses. It's aimed at the judge. If the judge asks, was the knife in his right hand, the witness now knows the court is looking for a knife in a right hand. The question teaches the lie. So the careful judge asks open questions, and lets the story come out on its own. The Talmud tells a story that shows how seriously Simeon took this. He once saw a man chase another man into a ruin. He ran in after them and found one man dying and the other holding a bloody sword. And Simeon said, in effect: either you killed him, or I did. But I can't convict you. The Torah needs two witnesses, and I only saw the sword, not the blow. Even when he was sure, he held himself to the court's rule. Questions shape what people tell you, and what you say you saw becomes someone else's truth.
screen: `SIMEON BEN SHETACH, A JUDGE.` · `QUESTION THE WITNESSES WELL.` · `YOUR QUESTION CAN TEACH THE LIE.` · `THE SWORD IN THE RUIN.` · then, large: `CAREFUL WORDS.`

segments.voice: Think of a conversation coming up where you want the truth, with a child, a coworker, a friend, and notice the question you'd normally ask, the one with the answer tucked inside it. Now, slowly, turn it into an open one: not, you finished it, right? Just, how did it go? Say it silently a few times, until it feels natural.
Careful words. Simeon ben Shetach's warning to judges: the way you ask can teach someone how to lie.
Your line: a question can teach a lie. The best questions don't carry an answer inside. Day two hundred forty-one, done.

242.title: Love the work (Avot 1:10)
242.hook: Shemaiah: love labor, hate lording over others, don't court the powerful
242.carry: half a wage, just to listen
242.howItsDone: Avot 1:10 is read as a teaching about the dignity of work, and some sages of the Mishnah and Talmud are remembered as people with trades as well as teachers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, careful words: Simeon ben Shetach, the judge who knew the way you ask can teach someone to lie. Your line was a question can teach a lie. Day two hundred forty-two.

A winter Friday in Jerusalem, a long time ago. A poor young laborer pays half his day's wage to get into the house of study. Today he has nothing left, so the guard won't let him in. He climbs onto the roof and lies down by the skylight, just to hear the teachers talk. Snow begins to fall. He stays. In the morning, the two teachers inside notice the room is strangely dark. They look up and find a man buried in snow across the window. The Talmud says they carried him down, warmed him by the fire, and said he was worth it. The young man was Hillel. One of his teachers was Shemaiah.
screen: `A WINTER FRIDAY.` → `HILLEL ON THE ROOF.` → `SHEMAIAH INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Shemaiah and his partner Avtalyon are the next pair in the chain of Pirkei Avot. The Talmud remembers that they came from families of converts, and they led the sages of their day. Shemaiah's saying has three short parts. First: love work. The Hebrew word is melakhah, the same word used for the creative work that stops on Shabbat. Not just tolerate it. Love it. Some of the sages had trades: Avot names a Rabbi Yochanan the sandal-maker, and elsewhere praises Torah study joined with work. For them, work wasn't a distraction from a holy life. It was part of one. Second: hate rabbanut. It sounds like being a rabbi, but here it means lording it over people, holding a title so others have to bow. Shemaiah had authority, and he warns against loving it. Third: don't get too close to the ruling power. Later in Avot, another sage warns that rulers draw people close when it suits them and drop them when it doesn't. Together: honest work, done gladly, without climbing over people, and without selling yourself to whoever's in charge. Now go back to the roof. Hillel spent half of every wage just to be let in to learn. He loved the work, both kinds: the labor that paid the fee, and the learning it paid for. And the teachers who found him didn't hand him a title. They warmed him up.

segments.voice: Picture a task waiting for you: a report, a sink of dishes, a shift, homework. Don't take in the whole mountain; find one small piece that's honestly good, like the feel of a clean counter, a problem that clicks, a customer you helped. Hold that piece in mind, and let yourself be glad of it.
Melakhah. Work, the same word used for the labor that stops on Shabbat: Shemaiah's call to love it, done gladly, with no lording over others.

243.title: Love peace, pursue peace (Avot 1:12)
243.hook: Hillel: be a disciple of Aaron, loving peace, loving people, drawing them near
243.howItsDone: Aaron is held up in Jewish teaching as the model peacemaker, and the Mishnah counts making peace between people (hava'at shalom) among the good deeds whose fruits a person enjoys in this world.

segments.voice: Yesterday, melakhah: Shemaiah's call to love the work, and Hillel lying in the snow by the skylight. Your line was half a wage, just to listen. Today, that young man on the roof grows up. Day two hundred forty-three.

Two friends have stopped talking. Maybe it was a wedding seating chart, maybe money, maybe one sharp text. You're friends with both, and you know the silence is hurting them both. The usual moves are two: pick a side, or carefully stay out of it. Pirkei Avot now reaches the poor laborer from the roof, all grown up. He's the last of the great pairs in the chain, alongside a sage named Shammai. And his first saying is about exactly this moment: two people who won't speak, and someone in the middle.
screen: `TWO FRIENDS, NOT TALKING.` → `PICK A SIDE, OR STAY OUT?` → `HILLEL.`

segments.voice: Hillel came to the land of Israel from Babylonia, poor and hungry to learn, and later tradition remembers him for his patience. His saying begins: be one of the disciples of Aaron, Moses's brother, the high priest. What kind of disciple? Loving peace and pursuing peace, loving people and drawing them near to the Torah. Why Aaron? The Torah never tells a story of Aaron making peace. The rabbis filled that silence. An early collection called Avot of Rabbi Natan says that when two people quarreled, Aaron would sit with one of them and say, your friend is heartbroken, he's ashamed of what he did to you. Then he would go to the other and say the same thing. And when the two met, they would embrace. Notice the verbs. Loving peace is a feeling. Pursuing peace is a chase. The Hebrew word is rodef, the word for running after something. Hillel may be echoing a psalm, which in the old Jewish Publication Society translation says, "Depart from evil, and do good; Seek peace, and pursue it." Peace doesn't come looking for you. You go after it, like Aaron walking from one house to the other. Then the last part: love people, and draw them near. Hillel's word means all creatures, every human being, not only the ones who already agree with you. He doesn't say push them toward the Torah. He says bring them close. A disciple of Aaron walks between people until they can find each other again.

segments.voice: Think of two people in your life who aren't getting along, family, coworkers, friends, and remember something good about each of them. Hillel. The sage from Babylonia who said: be a disciple of Aaron, love peace and chase it, love people and draw them near.

244.title: If not now, when? (Avot 1:14)
244.hook: Hillel: if I am not for myself, who is; if only for myself, what am I; if not now, when
244.carry: care for yourself, care beyond yourself
244.howItsDone: Hillel's three questions are among the best-known lines of Pirkei Avot, studied on summer Shabbat afternoons and often quoted in Jewish teaching as a call to act without delay.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hillel: be a disciple of Aaron, walking between two people until they meet. Your line was pursue peace. Today, Hillel asks three questions. Day two hundred forty-four.

There's a thing on your list that's been there for weeks. The call to your grandmother. The doctor's appointment. The apology. The form. Every morning it slides to tomorrow, and tomorrow is always a better day for it. About two thousand years ago, Hillel gave the shortest possible answer to that list. He didn't write it down; his students remembered it, and the Mishnah kept it. It's three questions, and it may be the most quoted saying in all of Pirkei Avot. It's on posters, in speeches, and Primo Levi borrowed it for the title of a novel. The last question is only four words in English.
screen: `THE THING ON YOUR LIST.` → `TOMORROW IS ALWAYS BETTER.` → `THREE QUESTIONS.`

segments.voice: Here is Hillel's saying, in chapter one. If I am not for myself, who will be for me? And when I am for myself, what am I? And if not now, when? The first question is about responsibility. Nobody else can live your life, learn your lessons, or do your good deeds for you. Commentators read it this way: if I don't work on myself, no one can do it in my place. It's not selfish. It's a person standing up. The second question turns right around. When I am only for myself, what am I? A person who lives only for himself shrinks. Hillel doesn't answer. He lets the question sit there, a little uncomfortable, for you to fill in. So the first two lines hold each other in balance: stand up for yourself, and don't stop there. The third line gives both of them a deadline. If not now, when? The Hebrew is im lo akhshav, eimatai. Akhshav is the ordinary word for now, the one people use to call a kid to dinner. No poetry in it. It means this minute. Some commentators add a sharper reading: now means this life, this world, while you still have time to act. The saying works like a staircase. Care for yourself. Care beyond yourself. Start today. Hillel, who climbed onto a roof in the snow rather than miss one lesson, knew what it meant not to wait for a better day.

245.title: Say little, do much (Avot 1:15)
245.hook: Shammai: make study regular, say little and do much, greet everyone cheerfully
245.howItsDone: A fixed daily or weekly time for Torah study, often with a study partner, is a long-standing Jewish practice, and 'receive everyone with a cheerful face' is taught as basic Jewish courtesy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, akhshav: now, this minute, the last of Hillel's three questions. Your line was care for yourself, care beyond yourself. Today, Hillel's partner. Day two hundred forty-five.

Two guests, one party. The first says, I'll bring a little something, and walks in with a tray of food that feeds the whole room. The second promises the moon in the group chat, and shows up with a bag of ice. Today's sage is Shammai, Hillel's partner in the chain. Later stories give him a reputation as the strict one, the one with the short temper, and you'll meet one of those stories in a few weeks. So his saying is a surprise. It ends with a smile.
screen: `A LITTLE SOMETHING, A WHOLE TRAY.` → `SHAMMAI, THE STRICT ONE.` → `A SAYING THAT ENDS WITH A SMILE.`

segments.voice: Shammai's saying has three parts. First: make your Torah fixed. Set a regular time for study and keep it, instead of learning only when you happen to feel like it. Second: say little and do much. The Talmud finds the model in Abraham. Three strangers come to his tent in the heat of the day, and he offers them, in his words, just a morsel of bread. Then he runs to the herd for a tender calf, has cakes baked from fine flour, and brings curd and milk. He promised a snack and served a feast. The rabbis say that's how the righteous behave: they promise a little and do a lot. Third, the surprise from the strict one: receive every person with a cheerful face. The Hebrew is be'sever panim yafot, literally with a pleasant, beautiful face. Every person, not only your friends or the important ones. An early rabbinic collection goes further: give someone the best gifts in the world with a sour face, and it's as if you gave nothing; greet them warmly with empty hands, and it's as if you gave them everything. A steady habit, quiet follow-through, and a warm face at the door. And that closes a week of sages: judge people favorably, kindness isn't the same as closeness, a question can teach a lie, half a wage, just to listen, pursue peace, care for yourself, care beyond yourself, and today, say little, do much.

segments.voice: Notice what your face is doing right now, maybe a little tight around the eyes, and let your jaw loosen and your forehead go soft. Then think of the next person you'll see, and picture greeting them the way you'd greet someone you've missed. Hold that picture, and let the warmth reach your face.
Say little. Shammai's rule, learned from Abraham: promise a little, do a lot, and greet every person with a cheerful face.
Your line: just a morsel of bread. Then came the whole feast. Two hundred forty-five days now.
